title: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
hook: Friday afternoon, a match, two flames, and hands over the eyes
tomorrow: you already speak a little Yiddish

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mezuzah, the words on the doorpost. Your line was take the words with you. Today, two small flames on a Friday.

Friday afternoon, and the clock is running. The oven's on, someone's still in the shower, a kid can't find their shoes. Then, at a minute printed on a calendar on the fridge, someone strikes a match and lights two candles. They circle their hands over the flames, cover their eyes, and whisper a blessing. When they look up, the week is over.
screen: `FRIDAY, THE CLOCK RUNNING.` → `TWO CANDLES.` → `HANDS OVER THE EYES.`

segments.voice: This is how Shabbat begins: the day of rest, from Friday sunset until the stars come out on Saturday night. Why sunset? In the Torah's first chapter, each day closes the same way: there was evening and there was morning. Evening comes first, so a day starts in the dark. And since lighting a fire is one of the kinds of work that stop on Shabbat, the candles go on while it's still light, in many towns eighteen minutes early, as a margin. Why two? The rest day is commanded twice, in two wordings: remember the day, and observe it. Zachor and shamor. One flame for each. Then the hands over the eyes. Usually you say a blessing and then do the thing. But once this blessing is said, Shabbat has begun, and no new fire can be lit. So people light first, cover their eyes, bless, and then look, as if the light were new. And why light at all? The rabbis said it's for shalom bayit, peace in the home: a light so the family can see each other's faces at dinner.
screen: `EVENING FIRST, THEN MORNING.` · `REMEMBER AND OBSERVE.` · `LIGHT, COVER, BLESS, LOOK.` · `PEACE IN THE HOME.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Look at the nearest light: a lamp, a window, even this screen. Breathe in. Close your eyes, the way people do after lighting. As you breathe out, open them slowly, as if the light were new.
The candles. Two flames before sunset on Friday: remember, and observe. Second word.
Your line: light, then rest. First the flame, then the week can stop. That's day two.

howItsDone: On Friday before sunset, many Jewish homes light two Shabbat candles (some add one for each child); the one lighting circles their hands over the flames, covers their eyes and says the blessing, then greets the family with Shabbat shalom.

myth: it starts at sunset on Friday: there was evening, and there was morning.
people cover their eyes because they light before the blessing

trapdoor: what you thought: candles to make dinner look nice.
what it means: the line where the week ends. two flames for remember and observe, lit before sunset because fire-making stops on Shabbat.

what a scholar hears: Exodus 20:8 says remember, Deuteronomy 5:12 says observe; Shabbat 23b puts the Shabbat lamp before even the Hanukkah lamp, for shalom bayit. the covered eyes solve a puzzle: light first, bless after.

story.title: the two angels at the door
story.text: Two angels follow a person home from synagogue on Friday night, one good and one bad. If they walk in and find the candles lit, the table set and the bed made, the good angel says: may it be like this next Shabbat too. And the bad angel, against its will, has to answer amen. If the house is dark and nothing's ready, it goes the other way around. Many families still sing to those two angels at the table.
story.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119b; the Friday-night song Shalom Aleichem

wrong.truth: it starts at sunset on Friday. in the Torah a day begins in the evening, so the candles come first.
